content: Prunus africana, also known as Pygeum africanum or simply Pygeum, has specific dosing recommendations based on its indications. It is important to consider the frequency of adverse effects, potential interactions, contraindications, and its use during pregnancy and lactation, as well as cost information. Traditionally, Pygeum has been used for a variety of conditions, including inflammation, kidney disease, urinary problems, malaria, stomachache, fever, difficulty urinating, mental disturbances, and inflammation of the prostate gland. Pygeum is likely effective in alleviating symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). However, it may be less effective compared to saw palmetto. It has been shown to reduce functional symptoms of BPH, including a 19% decrease in nocturia (frequent nighttime urination), a 23% increase in peak urine flow, and a 24% reduction in residual urine volume in men with BPH. Adverse effects associated with Pygeum include nausea and abdominal pain. Hypersensitivity reactions have also been reported. Regarding pregnancy, Pygeum is categorized as N/A due to insufficient data. Similarly, there is no available information on its safety during lactation. However, in general, it is considered acceptable for use, as controlled studies in pregnant women have not demonstrated evidence of fetal risk. There is no specific information available on the metabolism or excretion of Pygeum. Ferulic acid, a component of Pygeum, has been shown to reduce prostatic cholesterol levels. Additionally, phytosterols present in Pygeum inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which may contribute to its therapeutic effects.
